items.claim: A process reporting PID 1, its own network stack, hostname and IPC while running as root should be assumed namespaced, not host root, until the user namespace is checked.
items.body:
A process reporting PID 1, its own network stack, hostname and IPC while running as root should be assumed namespaced, not host root, until the user namespace is checked.

HackTricks reference: README (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HackTricks-wiki/hacktricks/master/src/linux-hardening/containers-namespaces/container-security/README.md)
items.disproof: Inspection shows an active user namespace that maps container root to a non-zero or unmapped host UID.

sources.quote: The process may believe it is PID 1, may believe it has its own network stack, may believe it owns its own hostname and IPC resources, and may even run as root inside its own user namespace.
The product performs an operation at a privilege level that is higher than the minimum level required, which creates new weaknesses or amplifies the consequences of other weaknesses.

For this reason, the REST API endpoint (used by the Docker CLI to communicate with the Docker daemon) changed in Docker 0.5.2, and now uses a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket bound on 127.0.0.1 (the latter being prone to cross-site request forgery attacks if you happen to run Docker directly on your local machine, outside of a VM).

items.claim: When the container has no user namespace or it is disabled, a root shell inside it is close to host root and the escape severity is much higher.
items.body:

items.claim: A Docker authorization policy that filters container creation but ignores docker exec, alternate JSON keys such as top-level Binds, or plugin administration leaves working privilege-escalation paths behind.
items.body:
A Docker authorization policy that filters container creation but ignores docker exec, alternate JSON keys such as top-level Binds, or plugin administration leaves working privilege-escalation paths behind.

HackTricks reference: authorization plugins (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HackTricks-wiki/hacktricks/master/src/linux-hardening/containers-namespaces/container-security/authorization-plugins.md)
items.disproof: The daemon rejects privileged docker exec, honors Binds restrictions, and blocks plugin management endpoints.

sources.quote: A plugin that blocks docker run --privileged but ignores docker exec, misses alternate JSON keys such as top-level Binds, or allows plugin administration may create a false sense of restriction while still leaving direct privilege-escalation paths open.
The product performs an operation at a privilege level that is higher than the minimum level required, which creates new weaknesses or amplifies the consequences of other weaknesses.

For this reason, the REST API endpoint (used by the Docker CLI to communicate with the Docker daemon) changed in Docker 0.5.2, and now uses a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket bound on 127.0.0.1 (the latter being prone to cross-site request forgery attacks if you happen to run Docker directly on your local machine, outside of a VM).

items.claim: The enforcement surface a hunter must probe is the full set: container creation endpoints plus HostConfig Binds, Mounts, Privileged, CapAdd, PidMode and namespace-sharing options, docker exec behavior, and plugin management endpoints.

items.disproof: Every one of those endpoints and HostConfig fields is validated against the policy and rejects out-of-model runtime actions.

sources.quote:
Common Plugin Targets

Important areas for policy review are:

- container creation endpoints
- HostConfig fields such as Binds, Mounts, Privileged, CapAdd, PidMode, and namespace-sharing options
- docker exec behavior
- plugin management endpoints
- any endpoint that can indirectly trigger runtime actions outside the intended policy model

Historically, examples such as Twistlock's authz plugin and simple educational plugins such as authobot made this model easy to study because their policy files and code paths showed how endpoint-to-action mapping was actually implemented.
The product performs an operation at a privilege level that is higher than the minimum level required, which creates new weaknesses or amplifies the consequences of other weaknesses.

For this reason, the REST API endpoint (used by the Docker CLI to communicate with the Docker daemon) changed in Docker 0.5.2, and now uses a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket bound on 127.0.0.1 (the latter being prone to cross-site request forgery attacks if you happen to run Docker directly on your local machine, outside of a VM).

items.claim: Creating an unconfined container and then requesting a privileged exec is a valid bypass test against policies that only block privileged container creation.
items.body:
Creating an unconfined container and then requesting a privileged exec is a valid bypass test against policies that only block privileged container creation.

HackTricks reference: authorization plugins (https://raw.githubusercontent.com/HackTricks-wiki/hacktricks/master/src/linux-hardening/containers-namespaces/container-security/authorization-plugins.md)
items.disproof: The daemon refuses the privileged exec request after an unconfined container is already running.

sources.quote:
Full Example: docker exec Adds Privilege After Container Creation

A policy that blocks privileged container creation but allows unconfined container creation plus docker exec may still be bypassed:

bash
docker run -d --security-opt seccomp=unconfined --security-opt apparmor=unconfined ubuntu:24.04 sleep infinity
docker ps
docker exec -it --privileged <container_id> bash


If the daemon accepts the second step, the user has recovered a privileged interactive process inside a container the policy author believed was constrained.
The product performs an operation at a privilege level that is higher than the minimum level required, which creates new weaknesses or amplifies the consequences of other weaknesses.

For this reason, the REST API endpoint (used by the Docker CLI to communicate with the Docker daemon) changed in Docker 0.5.2, and now uses a Unix socket instead of a TCP socket bound on 127.0.0.1 (the latter being prone to cross-site request forgery attacks if you happen to run Docker directly on your local machine, outside of a VM).
